An abundance of fresh gla- ciated exposure permitted an equitable spac- ing of cores (typically numbering 7-10) over several metres of outcrop at each site. In the laboratory samples were cut into 2.4 cm long cylinders. Magnetisations were measured be- fore and after alternating field (a.f.) and ther- mal treatment by 'minispin' and parastatic magnetometers. Cleaning steps by the a.f. method were 5 milliTesla (roT) to 30mT and then 10mT to peak fields of 140 mT. Cleaning steps by the thermal method were 100°C to 500°C and then in steps of 20 or 25°C to the Curie point of the magnetite (580°C) or he- matite (680 ° C) remanence carriers. Follow- ing examination of orthogonal vector projec- tions, components of magnetisation were resolved by principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980; Sherwood, 1989). With the exception of the lavas where the thermal method provided better component resolu- tion, both methods of treatment produced component definitions of comparable quality. Both earlier and later generations of the syenites have similar intensities of magnetisa- tion (Fig. 3). In addition to trachytes, the NE dyke suite includes basaltic members and some magnetisations are correspondingly stronger. The lavas, although of basaltic composition, have lower

It is recorded in the ~ 1100 Ma Mamainse Point lavas (Robertson, 1973 ) and in dyke swarms of the Thunder Bay district (Pesonen, 1979) of the Keweenawan igneous Province of North America. There is strong evidence from dyke contact zones in the latter example that the dykes record a primary TRM. It is unclear (cf. Palmer, 1970; Robertson, 1973 and Halls and Pesonen, 1983 ) whether more than one rever- sal is present in the Mamainse succession. The consistency of repeated asymmetry through eight field reversals in the Gardar succession and the component structure of the remanence (first subsection of third section, Pesonen, 1979 and Thomas and Piper, 1991 ) demon- strate that a secondary component com- pounded with a primary antiparallel axis is not an adequate explanation of asymmetry. Geo- magnetic implications of this observation are discussed by Nevanelinna and Pesonen ( 1983 ). Because the younger units in the Gar- dar Province are magnetised predominantly with one polarity equivalent to the westerly declinations (it is not at present possible to identify unambiguously the normal or re- versed sense of this magnetisation with respect to the present field) asymmetry cannot be re- cognised at later times in this area. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. PALAEOMAGNETIC DATA FOR THE ADELAIDE GEOSYNCLINE The palaeomagnetism of the Adelaide Geosyncline, including the Bunyeroo Formation containing the ejecta horizon, has been reported by McWilliams and McElhinny (1980). The Proterozoic and Early Palaeozoic rocks of the geosyncline were folded during the Late Cambrian-Ordovician Delamerian Orogeny. The Late Proterozoic (~600 Ma) Bunyeroo Formation is a fine-grained redbed horizon of marine-shelf origin. Such rocks are ideal for palaeomagnetic investigations. The direction of the cleaned magnetization component of the Bunyeroo Formation is of prefolding origin, which is evidence that its remanence may be original and dates from the time the strata were deposited. McWilliams and McElhinny (1980, table 2) listed possible primary poles from the Adelaide Geo- syncline. Table 1 gives an update of this list of primary poles. The pole for the Bunyeroo Formation is at latitude = 7°S and longitude = 17°E (dp = 9°, dm = 14°). As shown in Fig. 4, this is very close to the pole for the Acraman meltrock. McWilliams and McElhinny (1980) discussed the implications of the 50° difference in the pole positions between the Bunyeroo Formation and the underlying Brachina Formation. Their favoured interpretation was that the Bunyeroo Formation was remagnetized during the Middle to Late Cambrian, albeit before Delamerian folding; the Bunyeroo pole is quite distinct from Delamarian poles

INTRODUCTION The Acraman structure (Williams 1986, 1987, 1990) located in the Middle Proterozoic (~1590 Ma) Gawler Range Volcanics, South Australia (Fig. 1), is one of the largest known terrestrial impact structures. It is notable also as the likely source of a unique ejecta horizon of shock-deformed volcanic fragments within the Late Proterozoic (~600 Ma) Bunyeroo Formation of the Adelaide Geosyncline located 220-350 km east of the impact site (Gostin et al. 1986; Williams 1986) and within the correlative Lower Rodda Beds of the Officer Basin ~450 km northwest of the impact site (Wallace et al. 1989). The correlation of the Acraman structure with the Bunyeroo/Rodda ejecta horizon is based on the similarity of lithologies of the target and the ejecta material (both being dacitic), U-Pb zircon ages (Compston et al. 1987), and degree of shock metamorphism of ejecta clasts and rocks from the impact site, as well as the geographic distribution of the ejecta and lateral variation of clast size within the horizon (Gostin et al. 1986, 1990). Statistically indistinguishable late Silurian palaeolatitudes (Grampian terrane 27.0° S±3.5°; Northern Midland Valley terrane 22.9° S± 1.8°), comparable remagnetization histories, a shared 'normal' polarity for the primary magnetization and equivalent gyroremanence acquisition, favour correlation across the Highland Boundary Fault. Similar chemistry for biotite phenocrysts further corroborates correlation which was initially made on the basis of a similar field appearance and petrography. This correlation, together with evidence from provenance studies, suggests that the separation of the Northern Midland Valley and Grampian terranes inferred for the Ordovician period was largely removed by late Silurian times, with scope for relative displacements of the order of only tens of kilometres after Lower Old Red Sandstone deposition. 1. This study is of the latter type, and concerns the late displacement history of terranes juxtaposed by the Highland Boundary Fault (HBF) in central Scotland. The HBF juxtaposes Precamb

Palaeomagnetic tests of this hypothesis can be divided into two categories: those concerning the former separation of terranes (e.g. Van der Voo & Johnson, 1985; Trench, Bluck & Watts, 1988) and those which relate to the timing of their subsequent amalgamation and suturing. This study is of the latter type, and concerns the late displacement history of terranes juxtaposed by the Highland Boundary Fault (HBF) in central Scotland. The HBF juxtaposes Precambrian Dalradian meta- morphic rocks belonging to the Grampian terrane against the Ordovician Highland Border Complex and its unconformable Lower Old Red Sandstone (ORS) cover. We adopt the term Northern Midland Valley (NMV) terrane here to refer to the Highland Border Complex and its hidden extension beneath the Devonian and Carboniferous cover, recognizing that the Midland Valley itself may conceal important terrane boundaries. The Grampian and NMV terranes have demon- strably unrelated geological histories during Ordo- vician time and did not become unambiguously linked until late Devonian time (Bluck, 1985; Fig. 1). Introduction The displaced terrane hypothesis has been suggested to explain many aspects of the geology of the Caledonian-Appalachian system (e.g. Hutton, 1987; Bluck, 1985). Palaeomagnetic tests of this hypothesis can be divided into two categories: those concerning the former separation of terranes (e.g. Van der Voo & Johnson, 1985; Trench, Bluck & Watts, 1988) and those which relate to the timing of their subsequent amalgamation and suturing. This study is of the latter type, and concerns the late displacement history of terranes juxtaposed by the Highland Boundary Fault (HBF) in central Scotland. The HBF juxtaposes Precamb

stem (e.g. Hutton, 1987; Bluck, 1985). Palaeomagnetic tests of this hypothesis can be divided into two categories: those concerning the former separation of terranes (e.g. Van der Voo & Johnson, 1985; Trench, Bluck & Watts, 1988) and those which relate to the timing of their subsequent amalgamation and suturing. This study is of the latter type, and concerns the late displacement history of terranes juxtaposed by the Highland Boundary Fault (HBF) in central Scotland. The HBF juxtaposes Precambrian Dalradian meta- morphic rocks belonging to the Grampian terrane against the Ordovician Highland Border Complex and its unconformable Lower Old Red Sandstone (ORS) cover. We adopt the term Northern Midland Valley (NMV) terrane here to refer to the Highland Border Complex and its hidden extension beneath the Devonian and Carboniferous cover, recognizing that the Midland Valley itself may conceal important terrane boundaries. The Grampian and NMV terranes have demon- strably unrelated geological histories during Ordo- vician time and did not become unambiguously linked until late Devonian time (Bluck, 1985; Fig. 1). Introduction The displaced terrane hypothesis has been suggested to explain many aspects of the geology of the Caledonian-Appalachian system (e.g. Hutton, 1987; Bluck, 1985). Palaeomagnetic tests of this hypothesis can be divided into two categories: those concerning the former separation of terranes (e.g. Van der Voo & Johnson, 1985; Trench, Bluck & Watts, 1988) and those which relate to the timing of their subsequent amalgamation and suturing. This study is of the latter type, and concerns the late displacement history of terranes juxtaposed by the Highland Boundary Fault (HBF) in central Scotland. ent magnetization. If this magnetization is primary and about 150 m. y. ago, then the apparent northward displacement is on the order of 1,600 km (994 mi) with a clockwise rotation of 150 ± 25°. Again, the large uncertainties associated with the 150 m.y. paleopole render this apparent displacement insignificant. If, on the other hand, the magnetization is an overprint acquired about 90 to 100 m.y. ago during regional metamorphism and the tilt factor is negligible, then the implied displacement with respect to the 90 m.y. pole is 3,600 km (2,237 mi) with a clockwise rotation of 154 ± 16°. The fact that all the sites represented one polarity direction during a time interval when the polarity flipped several times (Tithonian to Valanginian) suggests that the magnetization is an overprint. The regional structural fabric is one of subhorizontal thrust sheets (Coleman, 1972), which indicates that the tilt factor may ·be negligible. However, because the magnetization may be the result of an anisotrophy associated with deformation, the tectonic implications of these results are limited. Only a slight improvement in the dispersion is seen after the beds were restored to horizontal. It appears that there is a more significant improvement in the inclination dispersion, which suggests either undetected structures not accounted for or localized independent rotations about near vertical axes. Only one polarity has been recognized in the Yolla Bolly terrane thus far, and it is possible that we are seeing an effect of metamorphic overprinting rather than an original sedimentary remanent magnetization. ent magnetization. If this magnetization is primary and about 150 m. y. ago, then the apparent northward displacement is on the order of 1,600 km (994 mi) with a clockwise rotation of 150 ± 25°. Again, the large uncertainties associated with the 150 m.y. paleopole render this apparent displacement insignificant. If, on the other hand, the magnetization is an overprint acquired about 90 to 100 m.y. ago during regional metamorphism and the tilt factor is negligible, then the implied displacement with respect to the 90 m.y. pole is 3,600 km (2,237 mi) with a clockwise rotation of 154 ± 16°. The fact that all the sites represented one polarity direction during a time interval when the polarity flipped several times (Tithonian to Valanginian) suggests that the magnetization is an overprint. The regional structural fabric is one of subhorizontal thrust sheets (Coleman, 1972), which indicates that the tilt factor may ·be negligible. However, because the magnetization may be the result of an anisotrophy associated with deformation, the tectonic implications of these results are limited. A bend in the block boundary is quite clear at about 23°30'N, 102°00'E: the strike of the Jinsha suture-Red River fault is N10°W - N35°W to the north of this point, whereas the strike of the Red River fault is N70°W to the south. Mesozoic rocks occur over a wide area around Chuxiong and Puchanghe in central Yunnan [26,27] and are mainly composed of purple sand- stones and siltstones. The Jurassic formations conformably underlie the Lower Cretaceous for- mations, which are followed disconformably by the Upper Cretaceous formations. The Creta- ceous system is divided into four successions, each well dated by fossils. In ascending order these successions are the Gaofengsi, Puchanghe, Matoushan and Jiangdihe Formations. Abstract New paleomagnetic data from Miocene (Altonian-Otaian) sediments from the northeastern part of the Raukumara Peninsula gave declinations close to those expected for the Australian plate (c. 20° for 20 Ma rocks), and imply that no net tectonic rotation has affected this region since that time, in contrast to the large declinations and large clockwise tectonic rotations previously recorded for the Gisbome-Wairoa region. The boundary between these two regions is constrained to lie within a broad 50 km zone between Tokomaru Bay and Gisbome. The expected inclination for 20 Ma rocks from the East Coast is 60° whereas for our localities the mean reversed inclinations are +35°; mean normal inclinations are -47°. This discrepancy may occur either during deposition by the alignment of the magnetic grains parallel to the sedimentation surface or during consolidation and compaction. Although early laboratory experimental studies (King 1955) have shown the existence of the former, it has rarely been observed in natural sediments. It is now generally considered that postdepqsitional realignment of the small, single-domain magnetio grains in the direction of the ambient field occurs (McElhinney 1973; Verosub 1977; Tarling 1982). The shallowing of the inclinations during compaction have been observed in sediments (Noltimier & Richardson 1980) and this is the most likely cause for the shallow inclinations observed here. Regardless of the causes of these apparent inclination errors the declination recorded in sediments is the magnetic parameter least influenced by depositional, postdepositional, andcompactional processes and should reliably record the magnetic field at the time the rock was formed. Box 600 Wellington, New Zealand Abstract New Zealand middle Pleistocene (Castlecliffian) rhyolitic tuffs older than 0.5 Ma are characterised on the basis of glass chemistry and paleomagnetism for the purpose of correlation. Of the tuffs examined, Rewa Pumice (c. 0.74 Ma), Potaka Pumice (c. 0.64 Ma), and Lower Te Muna Tephra (c. 0.75 Ma) are particularly widespread marker horizons. Their proven proximity to the Brunhes-Matuyama paleomagnetic reversal provides a useful framework for correlation and absolute age control between regions in southern North Island— Wanganui, Wairarapa, and Hawke's Bay—and with deep-sea cores from the Western Pacific. The tuffs allow correlation between a diverse range of sedimentary facies including marine, freshwater, and terrestrial, and provide absolute age control for thick sequences of unfossiliferous strata in Wairarapa and Hawke's Bay. The characterisation and correlation of the tuffs has a number of implications for Castlecliffian paleoclimatic, tectonic, and stratigraphic studies. The Rewa Pumice is contained in periglacial facies, and we assign it to oxygen isotope stage 20. Some tuffs in Hawke's Bay contain charcoal and are considered to be derived from ignimbrites. Their

tratotype along the Wanganui coast to sections across the Wanganui Basin, which contain radiometrically dated tuffs, are not sustainable, suggesting greater facies variations than hitherto assumed. The sequence of strata in the Rangitikei section containing the Rewa and Potaka Pumices is not a correlative of Kaimatira Pumice Sand at the coast section. Previous tuff correlations were made on the basis of age and mineralogy. Only the integrated use of glass chemistry and paleomagnetism allows correlation of tuffs in this time interval. Correlation between the regions is further hindered by the predominance of alluvial and lacustrine facies in southern Hawke's Bay and Wairarapa, which do not allow biostratigraphic correlation to mainly marine strata exposed in the Wanganui area. Numerous deep-sea cores from abyssal sediments in the Western Pacific, east of New Zealand, contain tuffs older than 0.5 Ma. Correlations to onshore sequences have been proposed based on tuff ages from magnetostratigraphically derived sedimentation rates and a few fission-track dates (Watkins & Huang 1977; Kyle & Seward 1984; Seward et al. 1986). These correlations have not been tested by glass chemistry. Relating the New Zealand Castlecliffian Stage to oxygen isotope stages (e.g., Beu & Edwards 1984; Kamp & Turner 1990) requires the p

tuffs in each region, as well as from two deep-sea cores, for the purpose of correlation. We attempt to extend the late Pleistocene tephrostratigraphic framework of Froggatt (1983) to strata older than 0.5 Ma. RESULTS Tectonic rotations of the northeastern South Island are reported with respect to the Pacific plate because this area is contiguous with the Pacific plate. Cenozoic paleomagnetic pole positions from the Pacific plate show no apparent polar wander (Grindley et al. 1977), indicating that the Pacific plate has not undergone significant rotation relative to true north since 35 Ma. The amount of tectonic rotation of a rock unit of age <20 Ma on the Pacific plate is therefore equal to the mean paleomagnetic declination minus the axial dipole declination (0° for normal polarity and 180° for reversed polarity), provided the mean inclination is equal to that expected at the sampling latitude for a geocentric axial dipole field. Paleomagnetic declinations divergent from those expected from the stable Pacific plate are referred to as "declination anomalies" and are interpreted as tectonic rotations about vertical axes. Useful tectonic rotation data were obtained from 10 localities including the 2 magnetostratigraphic localities, Blind River and Upton Brook. Laboratory procedure Measurements of magnetic remanence were made on a two- axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer at the Research School of Earth Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington, for most samples analysed. These samples were measured in four orientations and inverted and remeasured in four orientations. Data were rejected if the angular difference between averaged normal and inverted measurements exceeded 10°. Rock magnetic investigations of sediments in the lower Awatere Valley indicate that the major contributors to magnetic remanence are ferrimagnetic iron sulphide (pyrrhotite and greigite) and iron-titanium oxide minerals (Roberts 1990). These factors suggest that secular variation has been adequately averaged and that the observed declination anomalies are due to tectonic rotation about vertical axes. Standard errors associated with declin- ation anomalies are calculated following the approach of Demarest (1983). Rock magnetic investigations of sediments in the lower Awatere Valley indicate that the major contributors to magnetic remanence are ferrimagnetic iron sulphide (pyrrhotite and greigite) and iron-titanium oxide minerals (Roberts 1990). Dissolution of detrital titanomagnetite grains has occurred as a result of iron sulphide formation during early diagenesis, and the paleomagnetic signal due to titano- magnetite in such rocks is usually weak with significant remagnetisation having occurred. Samples where ferri- magnetic iron sulphide minerals are dominant are usually intensely and stably magnetised. It is therefore probable that iron sulphide minerals are largely responsible for the paleomagnetic signals recorded in this study. Available evidence suggests that sedimentary iron sulphide formation is severely restricted below the surface metre of marine sediments (Westrich & Berner 1984; Canfield & Berner 1987). RESULTS Tectonic rotations of the northeastern South Island are reported with respect to the Pacific plate because this area is contiguous with the Pacific plate. Cenozoic paleomagnetic pole positions from the Pacific plate show no apparent polar wander (Grindley et al. 1977), indicating that the Pacific plate has not undergone significant rotation relative to true north since 35 Ma. The amount of tectonic rotation of a rock unit of age <20 Ma on the Pacific plate is therefore equal to the mean paleomagnetic declination minus the axial dipole declination (0° for normal polarity and 180° for reversed polarity), provided the mean inclination is equal to that expected at the sampling latitude for a geocentric axial dipole field. Paleomagnetic declinations divergent from those expected from the stable Pacific plate are referred to as "declination anomalies" and are interpreted as tectonic rotations about vertical axes. Useful tectonic rotation data were obtained from 10 localities including the 2 magnetostratigraphic localities, Blind River and Upton Brook. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 73: 85—108. A magnetostratigraphic study of light-pink to’white pelagic limestones from the Bolücektasi Tepe section (southwestern Turkey) provides a magnetic polarity sequence well calibrated with the conodont zonation for the Lower Carnian and uppermost Carnian—Middle Norian (Late Triassic). Thermal (between 400 and 550°C) and alternating field (30—60 mT) demagnetizations isolate the characteristic remanent components. Rock magnetic experiments suggest that magnetite is the dominant magnetic carrier, but a small hematite fraction also exists in the Lower Carnian light-pink limestones. A major sedimentary gap (Middle—Upper Carnian) divides the section in two submembers which reveal two statistically different mean directions, differing in declination by about 30°. A sequence of 39 polarity intervals is obtained, 18 in the Carnian (ten in the Lower Carnian and eight in the uppermost Carnian) and 21 in the Lower—Middle Norian. It is reduced to some centimetres in the Valle delle Sfingi section, and has maximum thickness (3.13 m) in the Piccola Mantova II section. It is characterized by thin- bedded pink burrowed limestones commonly dis- playing wavy stratification (flaser-bedding). Some whitish layers showing planar geometry are inter- bedded with the flaser-bedded facies and locally display a planar lamination and/or small-scale cross-lamination partly obliterated by the biotur- bation. In thin section, these layers appear as microcoquinoid grainstones to grainstone/pack- stones, almost exclusively made up of thin-shelled bivalves. Cryptalgal fabrics, as well as evidence of early lithification are lacking in this member. The flaser bedding suggests that sediments remained in a soft state during the burial and consequently suffered stronger effects of burial diagenesis with respect to the nodular facies. The different diagen- etic history may explain the extreme scarcity of ammonite remains in this member, and their occurrence as deformed molds. Paleomagnetic analysis was done on specimens from 23 and 19 sites located in and around the Chipman Lake and Seabrook Lake complexes, respectively, using detailed alternating-field and thermal step demagnetization and isothermal remanent magnetization tests. ke's ChRM is retained in 11 dikes with normal polarity and one dike with reversed polarity and at one site with normal polarity and one site with reversed polarity from the fenite altera- tion zone. Its ChRM gives a pole position at 186"E, 38"N (dp = 7", dm = 11 "), which corresponds to a Keweenawan age of 1098 + 10 Ma, suggesting that younger K-Ar amphibole ages do not date emplacement. The ChRM of the host rock, the Chipman Lake diorite stock, gives a pole at 49OE, 51°N (dp = 8", dm = 13"), showing that it is not part of the Keweenawan complex but may be a 2.45 Ga Matachewan intrusive. The Seabrook Lake complex's ChRM is found at six normal polarity sites from within the complex and at four normal and three reversed polarity sites from within the fenitized Archean granite and Matachewan diabase of the contact aureole. It gives a pole position at 180°E, 46"N (dp = 11°, dm = 17"), which corresponds to a Keweenawan age of 1103 + 10 Ma, agreeing with K/Ar biotite ages. The paleomagnetic data indicate that no significant motion on the Kapuskasing Structural Zone occurred after emplacement of the complexes excluding minor vertical uplift of less than about 4 km, and that there were multiple polarity transitions of a symmetric Earth's magnetic field during Keweenawan time. An addi- tional two specimens from each site were thermally demagnet- ized in 10 steps to 615°C using a Schonstedt TSD-1 model thermal demagnetizer, with five additional steps for a few specimens to 690°C. The response of the remanence vector in the specimens from a given site was essentially the same for both AF and thermal step demagnetization, so the remaining specimens were AF demagnetized in four steps to best define their characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) direction over a broad coercivity spectrum of greater than 40 mT in most cases (Table 1). The ChRM directions have maximum angular deviations of less than 10" using principal component analysis, with most being less than 5" (Kirschvink 1980); these were combined using conventional tiered analysis to get the site mean directions (Fisher 1953). For a few sites the remagnetization circle method was used to estimate the rema- nence directions for some specimens, and these were com- bined with the ChRM directions to get the site means (Bailey and Halls 1984) (Table 1). One generalization is that the C component is easily iso- lated in these rocks after the initial VRM is removed by about 10 - 15 mT and 350-450°C on AF and thermal step demag- netization, respectively. A second generalization is that the ChRM directions of the lamprophyre and biotite dike sites tend to be somewhat better defined than in the fenite alteration zone or carbonatite and diabase dike sites, using the radii of their cones of 95 % confidence and precision parameters (k) as a measure (Fisher 1953). Nevertheless, the C com- ponent is clearly defined at all 14 sites. In almost all specimens magnetite with unblocking tempera- tures of less than 600°C is the significant carrier of C rema- nence (Fig. 7d). There are, however, a few specimens that retain a small C component in hematite with unblocking tem- peratures over 600°C (Fig. 7b). Introduction The Altiplano plateau at 4000m spreads between the Western and the Eastern cordil- lera of the Andes. The La Paz basin (Bolivia) situated at 16°30'S, 68°W (Fig.l) was cut in the Altiplano by a regressive erosional phase dur- ing the Late Pleistocene related to the setting of the upper hydrologic

logic basin of the Amazon. First reported by Troll and Finterwalter (1935), the lacustrine, fluvial and glacial deposits were described in detail by Dobrovolny (1962). The stratigraphy was recently reinterpreted by Servant (1977) and Ballivi&n et al. (1978). The first chronological data obtained on the post-Miocene deposits (5.5 Ma) results from K/Ar analyses on a tuff layer (Toba Umala) underlying the deposits in the Umala and Ayo Ayo basins, 100 km south from La Paz (Evern- den et al., 1977). This can be considered as a maximum age since remains of Pliocene roam- mals were discovered at Ayo Ayo, in the lower part of the Umala Formation, correlatable to the La Paz Formation (Hoffstetter, 1971), and at La Paz in the lower part of the La Paz formation (Villarroel, 1978). The K/Ar age was recently confirmed on a correlatable tuff layer near the base of the La Paz Formation called Toba Cota Cota: the age given by Servant et al. (1988) is 5.5_+0.02 Ma. Detailed demagnetization experiments on 114 samples from 17 sites yield two distinct groups of characteristic directions of the natural remanent magnetization. Component 'A', predominant in samples from the quartz syenitic central part and minor ring dyke of the complex, displays rather high blocking temperatures, well above 600 "C and is presumably carried by haematite. Mixed polarities of 'A' magnetization strongly suggest a Recent/pre-Brunhes age of this component, and the effects of long-term weathering and low-temperature oxidation. Component 'B', pointing to the southeast and upward, has been identified in seven sites from the major ring dyke, composed of aegirine syenite. G Complex geological and geophysical studies have shown that the structural arrangement of the pre-volcanic basement played an important role in the emplacement of the volcanic rocks in OIVT sector (Borcoa et al. 1979). The system of crustal faults of the pre-volcanic basement is represented in Fig. 2(a) after Skdulescu (1984). This system was probably tectonically active until Sarmatian and it is covered by the volcanic rocks and coeval sedimentary deposits. The volcanic activity took place during Late Miocene- Pliocene Period and had three main stages: (1) rhyolite- dacite tuffs and lava flows; (2) a succession of pyroxene- andesite and quartz-andesite strato volcanoes and lava flows; (3) pyroxene andesites and basaltic andesites forming strato volcanoes, which reach the collapse caldera stage (GiugcB et al. 1973). The age assigned for the volcanic rocks is based on the correlations with the sedimentary deposits of the surrounding basins. The ages of the sediments from the basins were determined according to the characteristic fauna for the Pannonian basin. In the sediments imbricated with the volcanic rocks, the fossils are rare, so the correlations with the sediments of the basins are based mainly on the facies similitude. the basins were determined according to the characteristic fauna for the Pannonian basin. In the sediments imbricated with the volcanic rocks, the fossils are rare, so the correlations with the sediments of the basins are based mainly on the facies similitude. Inside the volcanic areas when the sediments are absent the petrographic characteristics and the relative positions of the volcanic rocks were taken into account to assign the age. A complete review about the age of the volcanic rocks from OIVT sector was made by Borco? et al. (1973). For this study the Sarmatian, Pannonian and Pontian volcanic rocks of stages 2 and 3 were sampled. This local stratigraphic classification corresponds to the Tortonian and Messinian stages of the Late Miocene Period (Van Eysinga 1975). 650 block samples were collected from 199 sites in OIVT sector (Fig. 2). The block samples were oriented with a solar compass and in absence of sun, with a magnetic compass and a declination gradiometer (Doell & Cox 1962) to avoid the rocks subjected to lightning discharges. The system of crustal faults of the pre-volcanic basement is represented in Fig. 2(a) after Skdulescu (1984). This system was probably tectonically active until Sarmatian and it is covered by the volcanic rocks and coeval sedimentary deposits. The volcanic activity took place during Late Miocene- Pliocene Period and had three main stages: (1) rhyolite- dacite tuffs and lava flows; (2) a succession of pyroxene- andesite and quartz-andesite strato volcanoes and lava flows; (3) pyroxene andesites and basaltic andesites forming strato volcanoes, which reach the collapse caldera stage (GiugcB et al. 1973). The age assigned for the volcanic rocks is based on the correlations with the sedimentary deposits of the surrounding basins. The ages of the sediments from the basins were determined according to the characteristic fauna for the Pannonian basin. In the sediments imbricated with the volcanic rocks, the fossils are rare, so the correlations with the sediments of the basins are based mainly on the facies similitude. Received 1992 August 3; in original form 1992 March 30 SUMMARY For this palaeomagnetic study 199 sites were sampled in the northern part of the East Carpathians (Oag-Ignig-VZiratec-Tibleg sector). After AF (Alternating Field) demagnetization, 155 sites were selected for further analyses. A good agreement between the measured palaeomagnetic poles for the Pontian, the Pannonian and the reference polar wander path of Eurasia was made evident. In the southern part of the IgniS Mountains the Sarmatian volcanic rocks were affected by a 30" counter- clockwise rotation with respect to Europe post-emplacement. Key words: East Carpathians, Neogene magmatic rocks, palaeomagnetism, Romania. 1 INTRODUCTION On the territory of Romania a strong v

l arrangement of the pre-volcanic basement played an important role in the emplacement of the volcanic rocks in OIVT sector (Borcoa et al. 1979). The system of crustal faults of the pre-volcanic basement is represented in Fig. 2(a) after Skdulescu (1984). This system was probably tectonically active until Sarmatian and it is covered by the volcanic rocks and coeval sedimentary deposits. The volcanic activity took place during Late Miocene- Pliocene Period and had three main stages: (1) rhyolite- dacite tuffs and lava flows; (2) a succession of pyroxene- andesite and quartz-andesite strato volcanoes and lava flows; (3) pyroxene andesites and basaltic andesites forming strato volcanoes, which reach the collapse caldera stage (GiugcB et al. 1973). The age assigned for the volcanic rocks is based on the correlations with the sedimentary deposits of the surrounding basins. The ages of the sediments from the basins were determined according to the characteristic fauna for the Pannonian basin. In the sediments imbricated with the volcanic rocks, the fossils are rare, so the correlations with the sediments of the basins are based mainly on the facies similitude. the basins were determined according to the characteristic fauna for the Pannonian basin. In the sediments imbricated with the volcanic rocks, the fossils are rare, so the correlations with the sediments of the basins are based mainly on the facies similitude. Inside the volcanic areas when the sediments are absent the petrographic characteristics and the relative positions of the volcanic rocks were taken into account to assign the age. A complete review about the age of the volcanic rocks from OIVT sector was made by Borco? et al. (1973). Between these sectors the neogene volcanic rocks appear only sporadically. The previous palaeomagnetic studies were performed in the CGH sector (PBtravu 1976a). The results obtained from 85 sites yielded mean palaeomagnetic directions with D = 6" I = 62" aYg5 = 3" and k = 29, and allowed the separation of this sector into six areas according to the magnetic polarity. After AF (Alternating Field) demagnetization, 155 sites were selected for further analyses. A good agreement between the measured palaeomagnetic poles for the Pontian, the Pannonian and the reference polar wander path of Eurasia was made evident. Key words: East Carpathians, Neogene magmatic rocks, palaeomagnetism, Romania. 1 INTRODUCTION On the territory of Romania a strong v

of this domain are close to the island arc magmatites in their general petrochemistry (Pavelescu 1980; Balla 1985). The volcanic areas are in the inner side of the East Carpathians and in the Apuseni Mountains (Fig. 1). In the East Carpathians the Neogene volcanism is well developed in the northwestern part (Oa?, Ignia, Viiratec and Tiblea Mountains = OIVT sector) and in the southern part (CNimani, Gurghiu and Harghita mountains = CGH sector). Between these sectors the neogene volcanic rocks appear only sporadically. The previous palaeomagnetic studies were performed in the CGH sector (PBtravu 1976a). The results obtained from 85 sites yielded mean palaeomagnetic directions with D = 6" I = 62" aYg5 = 3" and k = 29, and allowed the separation of this sector into six areas according to the magnetic polarity. The emplacement of the studied volcanic rocks took place between 7Ma and 3Ma (RBdulescu, PBtraacu & Bellon 1972). The palaeomagnetic data are consistence with the absence of tectonic movements with respect to stable Europe post-emplacement. In this study the palaeomagnetic results from OIVT sector will be reported. 2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING Complex geological and geophysical studies have shown that the structural arrangement of the pre-volcanic basem

G Complex geological and geophysical studies have shown that the structural arrangement of the pre-volcanic basement played an important role in the emplacement of the volcanic rocks in OIVT sector (Borcoa et al. 1979). The system of crustal faults of the pre-volcanic basement is represented in Fig. 2(a) after Skdulescu (1984). This system was probably tectonically active until Sarmatian and it is covered by the volcanic rocks and coeval sedimentary deposits. The volcanic activity took place during Late Miocene- Pliocene Period and had three main stages: (1) rhyolite- dacite tuffs and lava flows; (2) a succession of pyroxene- andesite and quartz-andesite strato volcanoes and lava flows; (3) pyroxene andesites and basaltic andesites forming strato volcanoes, which reach the collapse caldera stage (GiugcB et al. 1973). The age assigned for the volcanic rocks is based on the correlations with the sedimentary deposits of the surrounding basins. The ages of the sediments from the basins were determined according to the characteristic fauna for the Pannonian basin. In the sediments imbricated with the volcanic rocks, the fossils are rare, so the correlations with the sediments of the basins are based mainly on the facies similitude. iable paleomagnetic poles (PPs) of early and mid-Paleozoic rocks in this continental block is thus very important for better understanding the tectonic evolution of southern South America. A sequence of Silurian-Devonian marine sedi- mentary rocks with intercalated ferriferous horizons, the Sierra Grande Formation, is exposed in north- eastern Patagonia. A preliminary paleomagnetic sampling of these rocks was carried out several years ago by one of the authors (JFV). The paleomagnetic study was started but, for technical reasons, could not be finished on that occasion. This study was finished recently, with the help of new and repaired instru- ments, as well as implementation of an integral com- puting system for paleomagnetism developed by Oviedo (1989). The results of this work, the first mid- Paleozoic paleomagnetic data from Patagonia, are reported here. A complete review of previous work and a description of this formation can be found in Zanettini (1981). Zanettini (1981) divided the Sierra Grande For- mation into two members. The lower, San Carlos Member consists of more than 500 ineters of marine quarzites, fine sandstones, siltstones, and shales. A complete review of previous work and a description of this formation can be found in Zanettini (1981). Zanettini (1981) divided the Sierra Grande For- mation into two members. The lower, San Carlos Member consists of more than 500 ineters of marine quarzites, fine sandstones, siltstones, and shales. A ferriferous horizon, the Rosales horizon, is inter- calated at about the middle of the sequence. This horizon, the thickness of which varies between 10 and 30 meters, is composed of oolitic hematite, but mag- netite has also been reported (Zanettini, 1981). The upper, Herrada Member, is composed of red to pink and brown coarse, medium, and fine sandstones and some siltstones, and is a minimum of 1000 meters thick. Another ferriferous horizon, the Alfaro hori- zon, is also intercalated near the bottom of the Herrada Member. iable paleomagnetic poles (PPs) of early and mid-Paleozoic rocks in this continental block is thus very important for better understanding the tectonic evolution of southern South America. A sequence of Silurian-Devonian marine sedi- mentary rocks with intercalated ferriferous horizons, the Sierra Grande Formation, is exposed in north- eastern Patagonia. A preliminary paleomagnetic sampling of these rocks was carried out several years ago by one of the authors (JFV). The paleomagnetic study was started but, for technical reasons, could not be finished on that occasion. This study was finished recently, with the help of new and repaired instru- ments, as well as implementation of an integral com- puting system for paleomagnetism developed by Oviedo (1989). The results of this work, the first mid- Paleozoic paleomagnetic data from Patagonia, are reported here. The formation is a mid- Paleozoic sedimentary sequence that covers the Pre- cambrian-early Paleozoic metamorphic and plutonic rocks constituting the North Patagonian Massif (Caminos and Llambias, 1984). A complete review of previous work and a description of this formation can be found in Zanettini (1981). Zanettini (1981) divided the Sierra Grande For- mation into two members. The lower, San Carlos Member consists of more than 500 ineters of marine quarzites, fine sandstones, siltstones, and shales. A ferriferous horizon, the Rosales horizon, is inter- calated at about the middle of the sequence. Another ferriferous horizon, the Alfaro hori- zon, is also intercalated near the bottom of the Herrada Member. This horizon is seldom thicker than 10 meters and is also composed mainly of oolitic hematite. The age of the Sierra Grande Formation has been determined accurately by studies of its fossils. According to Mancefiido and Damborenea (1984), the fossils found in the lower member (Iterrada) indicate a Wenlockian age. The age of the upper member (San Carlos) is not as well constrained. Although it has been assigned to the Early Devonian (Zanettini, 1981), Mancefiido and Damborenea have argued that the paleontologic record is too poor to accurately de- fine the age of the Herrada Member and that it could also be Late Silurian. The upper member, therefore is here conservatively considered as Late Silurian- Early Devonian. Accor

Paleomagnetic sampling was carried out only in the northern outcrop, because an important hydrothermal metamorphism, due to a late Paleozoic granitic intrusion, has widely affected the minera- logy of the ferriferous horizons in the southern expo- sure (GelSs, 1977; Zanettini, 1981). On the other hand, Avila (1980) and Zanettini (1981) have stated that "the original mineralogical characteristics of the depositional processes seem to be preserved in the ferriferous beds of the northern exposure." These are composed mainly of oolitic hematite, with minor proportions of chlorite and magnetite. All three components include normal and reversed sites. The A, B, and C poles are discordant with the positions expected for known metamorphic or intrusive events, but correction for a simple 37° clockwise rotation leads to concordancy of the A pole with the"" 175 Ma position, B with the"" 810 Ma position, and C with the"" 1400 Ma position on the APWP for the North American craton. These ages coincide with the known Laramide, Goat River, and East Kootenay orogenies. Evidently, the terrane housing the Purcell Anticlinorium: (1) has always been part of the North American craton with little or no translation; (2) was folded and metamorphosed in the East Kootenay orogeny prior to 1400 Ma; (3) was thermally overprinted in the Goat River orogeny; and (4) was thermally overprinted and then rotated"" 37°± 12° clockwise as Terrane I of the Cordillera impacted from the southwest against the craton during the mid-Mesozoic Laramide orogeny. INTRODUCTION The Middle Proterozoic Belt-Purcell Super­ group is exposed in southeastern British Columbia and in contiguous parts of Alberta, Montana, Idaho, and Washington (Figure 1). The Aldridge Forma­ tion in Canada and the equivalent Prichard Forma­ tion in the United States are stratigraphically near the base of the supergroup. The Moyie sills intrude the lower part of the Aldridge (Prichard) Formation. The study area is in the Purcell anticlinorium where paleomagnetic fold tests can indicate if a given remanence component was formed before or after folding. Paleomagnetic analysis was done on specimens from 27 sites in layered argillites of the Aldridge and from 30 sites in the Moyie metagabbros using AF and thermal (Th) demagnetization methods. Fold and contact tests show that no primary remanence components were isolated. However, three post­ folding metamorphic components were found: A was found in 9 argillite (AF, 22.9°, 64.1°, u95 = 9.8°) and 11 sill sites (AF, 35.2°, 62.0°, U95 = 7.1°); B was found in 8 argillite (AF, 320.4°, 52.0°, U95 = 11.8°) and 10 sill sites (Th, 303.6°, 56.9°, U95 = 7.8°); and C was found in 19 argillite sites (AF, 209.0°, 3.1°, U95 = 6.0°). All three components include normal and reversed sites. The A, B, and C poles are discordant with the positions expected for known metamorphic or intrusive events, but correction for a simple 37° clockwise rotation leads to concordancy of the A pole with the"" 175 Ma position, B with the"" 810 Ma position, and C with the"" 1400 Ma position on the APWP for the North American craton. These ages coincide with the known Laramide, Goat River, and East Kootenay orogenies. Evidently, the terrane housing the Purcell Anticlinorium: (1) has always been part of the North American craton with little or no translati

hermally overprinted in the Goat River orogeny; and (4) was thermally overprinted and then rotated"" 37°± 12° clockwise as Terrane I of the Cordillera impacted from the southwest against the craton during the mid-Mesozoic Laramide orogeny. INTRODUCTION The Middle Proterozoic Belt-Purcell Super­ group is exposed in southeastern British Columbia and in contiguous parts of Alberta, Montana, Idaho, and Washington (Figure 1). The Aldridge Forma­ tion in Canada and the equivalent Prichard Forma­ tion in the United States are stratigraphically near the base of the supergroup. The Moyie sills intrude the lower part of the Aldridge (Prichard) Formation. The study area is in the Purcell anticlinorium where paleomagnetic fold tests can indicate if a given remanence component was formed before or after folding. The object of the study was to determine if this Precambrian terrane was rotated or translated relative to the North American craton, as was found in Mesozoic rocks of Terrane I of the Cordillera to the immediate west (Symons and Litallien, 1984). A comparison of Tertiary Coast Belt paleopoles demonstrates that they are systematically rotated clockwise and are near- sided relative to the cratonic reference poles. This implies that the Coast Belt has been displaced 300 km southward and rotated 8" clockwise, or regionally tilted downward to the northwest, or some combination of these two end members, since the Late Miocene. These scenarios appear untenable. Evidence is given that the directional bias of the paleopoles is caused by unremoved present Earth's magnetic field (PEMF) overprint magnetizations, which comprise 10-25 % of the total remanence in most cases. The implication is that demagnetization and analysis techniques used in previous Tertiary Coast Belt studies, to varying degrees, may have insufficiently removed the PEMF overprints. The case is made for the importance of thorough alternating field and thermal step demagnetization, of all specimens, in order to maximize magnetic component data from which the principal magnetic components can be best isolated and PEMF components removed. Paleomagnetism of the Middle Miocene Rogers Creek pluton (16 Ma) in the central-southern Coast Belt was utilized to test the tilt hypothesis. Well-grouped stable primary magnetizations have been isolated in 11 sites with both normal and reverse polarities. The mean remanence component, directed at D = 000.7', I = 67.9" (a,, = 3.9", paleolatitude 50.9 f 9"N, paleopole 88.3"N, 257.5"E, A,, = 5.7"), was likely acquired upon emplacement at 16 Ma. This direction agrees with the Middle Miocene reference direction (D = 357", 1 = 68") calculated from the updated Miocene (10-20 Ma) cratonic reference pole for North America. This concordant result, when combined with concordant data from other mid- Tertiary intrusions to the south, defines a southern Coast Belt domain that shows no evidence of post-Middle Miocene tectonic tilt. This result does not preclud

estigating crustal tilts in the Coast Belt. A comparison of Tertiary Coast Belt paleopoles demonstrates that they are systematically rotated clockwise and are near- sided relative to the cratonic reference poles. This implies that the Coast Belt has been displaced 300 km southward and rotated 8" clockwise, or regionally tilted downward to the northwest, or some combination of these two end members, since the Late Miocene. These scenarios appear untenable. Evidence is given that the directional bias of the paleopoles is caused by unremoved present Earth's magnetic field (PEMF) overprint magnetizations, which comprise 10-25 % of the total remanence in most cases. The implication is that demagnetization and analysis techniques used in previous Tertiary Coast Belt studies, to varying degrees, may have insufficiently removed the PEMF overprints. The case is made for the importance of thorough alternating field and thermal step demagnetization, of all specimens, in order to maximize magnetic component data from which the principal magnetic components can be best isolated and PEMF components removed. It is very unlikely that inadequate averaging of secular variation would introduce a systematic effect consistent with both polar- ities. Furthermore, in this study detailed step demagnetization of specimens yields univectorial decay after remove1 of "soft" magnetizations (Figs. 7, 8), indicating that significant residual PEMF overprints seem unlikely. Long-term asymmetries in the EMF appear to be the most salient explanation in view of the abundant evidence suggesting the existence of biased nondipole components for perhaps the last 100 Ma (e.g., Merrill et al. 1979; Coupland and Van der Voo 1980). Palcomagnetic data from pillow basalt and sheeted dikes of the ophiolite yield a mean palcolatitude of 540_+7 ø, which implies 13_+9 ø of poleward displacement. The characteristic component of the remanence resides in a Ti-poor titanomagnetite with a blocking temperature close to 580øC. A positive fold test and the petrology of the magnetic minerals lead us to conclude that the characteristic reinanent magnetization (ChRM) in the sheeted dikes originated as a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). We hypothesize that the ChRM of the pillow basalt originated as a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) acquired soon after formation of the rocks during hydrothermal metamorphism. In the eastern gulf, Chugach terrane rocks are generally more deformed and metamorphosed than the Prince William terrane rocks. In the western gulf, complex lithologic and structural relationships, a paucity of age control, and no distinctive petrographic breaks combine to obscure the terrane boundary. Due to this ambiguity in terrane distinction in the western gulf, we herein treat the two terranes as one: the Chugach-Prince William terrane. We envision a history where extrusion and quenching of pillow basalt with typical titanomagnetite (x = 0.6) was followed by low-temperature oxidation to produce titanomaghemite. Preliminary results based on three sites of Late Permian to Early Triassic sediments from northern Bolivia also show a large counterclockwise rotation. The observed differences between the primary and the secondary magnetization indicate that large block rotations occurred prior to the acquisition of the secondary magnetization. Perhaps, this first episode of deformation partially structured the Andean chain in the Central Andes and induced an incipient orocline. During the Cenozoic, a differential shortening along the chain gave the present-day shape of the Bolivian deflection and resulted in a counterclockwise rotation of the forearc system by about 20 ø as indicated by the remagnetization. Twenty-six samples were selected for petrographic studies. Hematite (site PE01) is observed as a product of deuteric oxidation (classes 4 and 5 as defined by Haggerty [1976]). Peruvian coastal batholith from the Arequipa area. Five sites of the Chocolate volcanic formation were sampled near Ilo. Three sites in nearby intrusive formations were also sampled, but only one site (PE34) in the Punta Coles diorite has a stable remanent magnetization. Fourteen sites were collected in andesitic to rhyolitic flows, sills, and dikes in the area of La Yarada, west of the city of Tacna. Measurements of the remanence have been performed on a DSM1 Schonstedt spinner magnetometer. Alternating field (AF) demagnetizations were performed with a GSD1 Schonstedt demagnetizer. The residual field in the furnace used for the thermal demagnetization was less than 10 nT. Magnetic Properties Large variations in magnetic properties are observed between sites as indicated by the geometric mean values per site of the magnetic susceptibility and the intensity of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) listed in Table 2. In particular, low intensities of magnetization (about 0.01 A m -1) and low susceptibility values are observed in several sites from the volcanic units. There is no convincing evidence for opaque granulation or opaque pseudomorphs by black titanite, characteristic of burial metamorphism lAde-Hall et al., 1971]. However, at sites PE09 and PE10, the clinopyroxene is replaced by chlorite, calcite, hematite, futile, and titanite whereas the plagioclase is altered to albite, white mica, and, locally, pumpellyite and epidote. is replaced by chlorite, calcite, hematite, futile, and titanite whereas the plagioclase is altered to albite, white mica, and, locally, pumpellyite and epidote. Therefore these rocks have probably suffered a nondeformational, low-grade alteration of hydrothermal-burial type (spilitization) in the zeolite and prehnite-pumpellyite facies as is well documented in adjacent regions [Palmer et al., 1980b; Aguirre and Offer, 1985; Aguirre, 1988]. At Ilo and La Yarada, the magmatic paragenesis is generally not preserved. Plagioclases, clinopyroxenes, and olivines are completely transformed to actinolite, chlorite, calcite, epidote, and hematite associations. Textures of primary or high- temperature deuteric alteration were obliterated in opaque minerals. Hematite occurs as homogeneous large crystals and as minute disseminated phases in pseudomorphosed phenocrysts and in the groundmass. Near Ilo, numerous hematite-bearing veins crosscut the Chocolate Formation. Tourmaline occurs as a hydrothermal product in the volcanic breccias. These features indicate that contact metamorphism has occurred in the Ilo and La Yarada areas. Counterclockwise rotations of 50 ø to 80 ø are documented near the localities of Chala (eight sites), Ocon (two sites) and Arequipa (four sites). Preliminary results based on three sites of Late Permian to Early Triassic sediments from northern Bolivia also show a large counterclockwise rotation. The observed differences between the primary and the secondary magnetization indicate that large block rotations occurred prior to the acquisition of the secondary magnetization. Perhaps, this first episode of deformation partially structured the Andean chain in the Central Andes and induced an incipient orocline. During the Cenozoic, a differential shortening along the chain gave the present-day shape of the Bolivian deflection and resulted in a counterclockwise rotation of the forearc system by about 20 ø as indicated by the remagnetization. Therefore these rocks have probably suffered a nondeformational, low-grade alteration of hydrothermal-burial type (spilitization) in the zeolite and prehnite-pumpellyite facies as is well documented in adjacent regions [Palmer et al., 1980b; Aguirre and Offer, 1985; Aguirre, 1988]. At Ilo and La Yarada, the magmatic paragenesis is generally not preserved. Plagioclases, clinopyroxenes, and olivines are completely transformed to actinolite, chlorite, calcite, epidote, and hematite associations. Textures of primary or high- temperature deuteric alteration were obliterated in opaque minerals. Hematite occurs as homogeneous large crystals and as minute disseminated phases in pseudomorphosed phenocrysts and in the groundmass. Near Ilo, numerous hematite-bearing veins crosscut the Chocolate Formation. Tourmaline occurs as a hydrothermal product in the volcanic breccias. These features indicate that contact metamorphism has occurred in the Ilo and La Yarada areas. This contact metamorphism is produced by the Jurassic and Cretaceous plutonism and is superimposed onto the low-grade alteration of hydrothermal-burial

We found component A (northwest and shallow direction) in the Hound Island Volcanics exposed at Cape Bendel on Kupreanof Island, on Turnabout Island, and also on one of the Keku Islets (Figure 2). This component was not observed by Hillhouse and Groinrod [ 1980], nor did we find it at any of the sites we sampled that were previously studied by Hillhouse and Groinrod [1980], which are 14 km south of Cape Bendel. In addition, we found this component only in rocks from lava flows and pyroclastic deposits, not in pillow lavas and pillow breccias. The component A directions pass a fold test, indicating the magneti- zation was acquired before folding of the strata. Although the major regional deformation occurred in Late Cretaceous time, we think that the metamorphism of the Hound Island Volcanics occurred on the seafloor soon after eruption. Our main reasons are that chlorite, calcite, prehnite, and other unidentified green minerals fill vesicles. The 40Ar/39Ar analyses on samples of the Hound Island Volcanics, which we discuss later in this paper, also indicate that the major metamorphism occurred soon after deposition. Finally, an anomalously large 87Sr/86Sr ratio from one sample on Hound Island (Figure 2) is most easily understood if there was intensive seawater interaction with the lava [Samson et al., 1989], consistent with hydro- thermal alteration of the lavas on the seafloor. ent A: Northwest and Shallow Direction Directional data. We found component A (northwest and shallow direction) in the Hound Island Volcanics exposed at Cape Bendel on Kupreanof Island, on Turnabout Island, and also on one of the Keku Islets (Figure 2). This component was not observed by Hillhouse and Groinrod [ 1980], nor did we find it at any of the sites we sampled that were previously studied by Hillhouse and Groinrod [1980], which are 14 km south of Cape Bendel. In addition, we found this component only in rocks from lava flows and pyroclastic deposits, not in pillow lavas and pillow breccias. The component A directions pass a fold test, indicating the magneti- zation was acquired before folding of the strata. The data pass the stan- dard regional tilt test of McElhinny [1964] at 82% confidence (Figure 4). Although the major regional deformation occurred in Late Cretaceous time, we think that the metamorphism of the Hound Island Volcanics occurred on the seafloor soon after eruption. Our main reasons are that chlorite, calcite, prehnite, and other unidentified green minerals fill vesicles. The 40Ar/39Ar analyses on samples of the Hound Island Volcanics, which we discuss later in this paper, also indicate that the major metamorphism occurred soon after deposition. Finally, an anomalously large 87Sr/86Sr ratio from one sample on Hound Island (Figure 2) is most easily understood if there was intensive seawater interaction with the lava [Samson et al., 1989], consistent with hydro- thermal alteration of the lavas on the seafloor. The Point Camden Gabbro The Hound Island Volcanics were intruded by 23-Ma gabbroic intrusions in the Keku Strait. We will informally refer to this unit as the Point Camden gabbro because of outcrop exposures at Point Camden on Kuiu Island (Figure 2). Although the major regional deformation occurred in Late Cretaceous time, we think that the metamorphism of the Hound Island Volcanics occurred on the seafloor soon after eruption. Our main reasons are that chlorite, calcite, prehnite, and other unidentified green minerals fill vesicles. The 40Ar/39Ar analyses on samples of the Hound Island Volcanics, which we discuss later in this paper, also indicate that the major metamorphism occurred soon after deposition. Finally, an anomalously large 87Sr/86Sr ratio from one sample on Hound Island (Figure 2) is most easily understood if there was intensive seawater interaction with the lava [Samson et al., 1989], consistent with hydro- thermal alteration of the lavas on the seafloor. If the rocks cool through this temperature range in a few thousand years or less, then a single specimen or locality would not completely aver- age secular variation. For example, Dodson et al. [1978] contended that because such a record is present, cooling rates in the pluton were fast enough to go through the blocking temperature range of the samples in a short period of time. POINT CAMDEN GABBRO Introduction The Keku Strait separates Kuiu from Kupreanof Island in southeastern Alaska (Figure 2). Muffler [1967] mapped the geology in the area, finding stratified units that range in age from Silurian to Tertiary, and Tertiary gabbroic dikes and sills. There are large exposures of this Tertiary gabbro at Point Camden on Kuiu Island (Figure 2), and we will informally refer to it as the Point Camden gabbro. The gabbro is olivine and clinopyroxene bearing, and medium grained. Muffler [1967] suggested that these intrusions are gently dipping sills up to 450 m thick. He noted that an uncommon magmatic foliation in the gabbro was roughly parallel to the strike of gently dip- ping bedding in the Tertiary Kootznahoo Formation, which it intrudes, and that the outcrop pattern of the gabbro is roughly parallel to the strike of the Kootznahoo Formation. In Apulia (southern Italy), 11 quarries in late Pliocene and early Pleistocene clays were sampled to study the rotation of the underlying Apulian Unit. To analyze the Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) of the samples thermal magnetization was performed. Several NRM-com- ponems were distinguished. The component removed be- tween 350-380øC and 450-480øC is the most consistent one; it also shows a positive reversal test. There is no rotation for this so-called HT-component. Mean inclination is the same as the inclination of the geocentric axial dipole (GAD) field for the present latitude of the area. stratigraphy of the Ilerdian stratotype locality—the Tremp section, Spain—has been established. In total, 315 samples from 66 levels have been demagnetized, both thermally and by alternating field. East of the Central Coal basin, the upper member is made up of nodular, glauconitic limestones which are very rich in echinoderm debris. To the south and west of the basin, the upper member consists of a red, fine-grained nodular limestone, devoid of echino- derm debris. This latter facies was sampled. The sites are concentrated in the south and west because the Lancara Formation does not crop out where the tectonic style changes from thrust- ing to folding. The As- turian arc is a thin-skinned fold-thrust belt, which is concave towards the foreland and whose struc- tures face inwards. The structural trend varies by about 180” around the arc. The western boundary of the Asturian arc is the Narcea antiform (Fig. 11. The geology of the area is fairly we11 known, and maps on the scale 1 : 50,000 are available for the whole area. of the thrust sheets and the irregularities produced by hanging-wall ramp anticlines, duplexes and an- tiformal stacks, made motion difficult. Sixteen new Jurassic and Cretaceous paleomagnetic sampling sites are located in northern Umbria along three river valleys (Basso, Burano, Sentino). The Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous data are consistent in declination, but not inclination, with previously published data from these valleys. Early Jurassic data from eight sites give site mean declinations which are significantly different from the two site mean declinations of this age which were previously available. Comparison of the data with Cretaceous and Jurassic mean directions from the Southern Alps indicate 20” anticlockwise rotation, relative to the Southern Alps, of this part of northern Umbria during Neogene deformation of the Umbrian fold and thrust belt. leomagnetic sampling sites are located in northern Umbria along three river valleys (Basso, Burano, Sentino). The Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous data are consistent in declination, but not inclination, with previously published data from these valleys. Early Jurassic data from eight sites give site mean declinations which are significantly different from the two site mean declinations of this age which were previously available. Comparison of the data with Cretaceous and Jurassic mean directions from the Southern Alps indicate 20” anticlockwise rotation, relative to the Southern Alps, of this part of northern Umbria during Neogene deformation of the Umbrian fold and thrust belt. If the Umbrian mean directions are rotated to compensate for the tectonic rotation, the Early Jurassic and Cretaceous Umbrian and Southern Alpine pole positions coincide closely with a recently derived African apparent polar path (APWP). implying that Adria moved with Africa since at least Early Jurassic times. The Late Jurassic Umbrian and Southern Alpine poles, however, are not consistent with current APWPs and imply rapid apparent polar wander (in both African and North American coordinates) from high latitude to lower latitude between Bathonian and Oxfordian times.
